cards.title: What is an **operating system** (OS), and what is its **kernel**?
cards.body:
Software that shares the CPU, memory and devices among programs and hides the hardware behind a simple interface; the kernel is its always-loaded core.

The OS has three main jobs: share the CPU among many programs, give each program its own view of memory, and manage devices (disk, network, timers) so programs don't have to drive them directly.

The **kernel** is the part that is always in memory and does those jobs with full control of the hardware. Tools such as the shell and the file manager ship with the OS but are ordinary programs, not part of the kernel.

Why it matters: Without an OS, every program would have to talk to the hardware itself and could overwrite any other program's memory.

Tip: Many microcontrollers run firmware with no OS at all, and others run a tiny kernel that offers little more than scheduling and synchronization. The jobs above are the full picture, and small systems implement only some of them.
cards.searchQuery: what is an operating system kernel jobs

cards.title: What is the difference between **user mode** and **kernel mode**?
cards.body:
In kernel mode the CPU may run every instruction and touch all memory and devices; in user mode it may not.

The CPU keeps a mode in a hardware flag. Ordinary programs run in user mode. The kernel runs in kernel mode, which is also called privileged or supervisor mode.

Why: If any program could change page tables, switch off the timer or write to the disk controller, one buggy program could take down the whole machine. User mode makes those actions illegal, so a program that tries one is stopped.

Example: RISC-V defines three privilege levels: user (U), supervisor (S) and machine (M). A general-purpose OS such as Linux runs its kernel in S mode and its programs in U mode.

Watch out: Kernel mode does not mean "faster" or "more memory". It only widens which instructions and addresses are allowed.
cards.searchQuery: user mode versus kernel mode privileged CPU

cards.title: What is a **process**?
cards.body:
A running instance of a program, with its own address space, registers and open files.

A program is a file on disk; a process is that program being executed. Start the same program twice and you get two processes. The kernel tracks each process's registers, program counter, open files and **address space**: the set of addresses the process can use.

Why it matters: Each process sees its own addresses, and the same virtual address in two processes usually maps to different physical memory. That is how one program's bug stays out of another program.

Watch out: A process is not the same as a program. A process also has state that changes as it runs: its registers, its stack and its heap.
cards.searchQuery: what is a process program versus process address space

cards.title: In which three **process states** can a process be?
cards.body:
Running (on a CPU), ready (able to run but waiting for a CPU) and blocked (waiting for something, such as input, so it cannot run yet).

The **scheduler**, the part of the kernel that picks what runs next, moves a ready process to running. A running process goes back to ready when its turn ends, or to blocked when it asks for something slow, such as a disk read. When that request finishes, the process becomes ready again, not running directly.

Example: A text editor waiting for a keypress is blocked and uses no CPU time. When you press a key, it becomes ready and runs as soon as the scheduler picks it.

Tip: On Linux, `ps aux` shows the state in the STAT column: `R` is running or ready, `S` is sleeping (blocked, waiting for an event), `D` is blocked in uninterruptible sleep, `Z` is a finished process whose parent has not collected it yet. `top` shows the same letters in its S column.

refs: Linux man page ps(1), section Process State Codes

cards.body:
`child`, then `parent`, on two lines, in that order every time.

`fork()` creates a new process that is a copy of the caller, and it returns twice: 0 in the child, and the child's process ID (a positive number) in the parent. So `pid == 0` is true only in the child.

`wait(NULL)` makes the parent block until a child process has exited. That forces the child's line to come first.

Watch out: Without `wait`, the order is up to the scheduler, so the output could come in either order. A parent that never waits also leaves finished children as zombies (the `Z` state in `ps`).

cards.body:
`child x=99`, then `parent x=10`.

After `fork`, the child has its own copy of the parent's address space, so it also has its own `x`. The child's write changes only its copy.

Why it works: Copying every page at `fork` would be slow. Real kernels use **copy-on-write**: parent and child share the same physical pages, marked read-only in the page tables, and the kernel copies a page only when one of them writes to it.

Key idea: Processes do not share variables through `fork`. If they need to share data, they must ask the kernel for it (a pipe or shared memory), while threads share memory directly (see the Threads unit).

cards.body:
`before`, then `hello`. The line `after` is never printed.

**exec** replaces the running program's code, stack and heap with those of a new program, in the same process (same process ID). If the call succeeds, the old program is gone, so `exec` never returns and `printf("after\n")` is never reached. It returns, with -1, only when it fails, for example when the program isn't found.

Example: A shell runs a command in three steps: it calls `fork`, the child calls `exec` to become the new program, and the shell calls `wait`. Redirection such as `ls > out.txt` works because the child changes its standard output between `fork` and `exec`.

Watch out: The `fflush(stdout)` matters. Text still sitting in the output buffer is discarded when `exec` replaces the process, so without the flush `before` can disappear when stdout is a file or pipe.

cards.title: What is a **system call**, and how does a call such as `write()` reach the kernel?
cards.body:
A request from a user program asking the kernel to do something privileged for it, such as reading a file or sending bytes to a device.

The C function `write()` is a thin library wrapper. It puts the system-call number and the arguments in registers, then runs a special **trap** instruction. The CPU switches to kernel mode and jumps to a kernel handler, which does the work, puts the result in a register and returns to user mode just after the trap instruction.

Example: On RISC-V Linux the wrapper loads the call number into `a7` and the arguments into `a0` to `a5`, then executes `ecall`. When the kernel returns, the result is in `a0`.

Key idea: A trap is any transfer of control from running code into the kernel's handler. A system call is the deliberate kind, requested by the program itself.
cards.searchQuery: system call write wrapper trap instruction kernel mode

cards.body:
`write(1, "hi\n", 3) = 3`

**strace** runs a program and prints every system call it makes, with its arguments and return value. Here `printf` formats the text in user mode and then calls `write` on file descriptor 1 (a small number the kernel uses to name an open file; 0, 1 and 2 are stdin, stdout and stderr). It asks for 3 bytes (`h`, `i`, newline) and the kernel reports that it wrote 3. Real `strace` pads the line with spaces before the `=` so the results line up in a column.

Watch out: On a terminal, the program's own `hi` is printed while `strace` is still in the middle of the line, because the call is shown before it runs and the result after. You see `write(1, "hi\n", 3hi`, then a line starting `) = 3`. Use `strace -o trace.txt` to keep the trace in a separate file.

Tip: Run `strace ./hello` without the filter and you will see many more lines first: `execve` that starts the program, and calls such as `brk` and `mmap` that set up its memory.

Watch out: When stdout is a file or pipe, `printf` keeps the text in a buffer and writes it all at exit. You still see the same `write` call, but it appears later and may carry many lines at once.
cards.searchQuery: strace -e trace=write printf hello system call output
refs: MIT Missing Semester 2026: Debugging and Profiling

cards.body:
`-1`

File descriptor -1 does not name an open file, so the kernel refuses the request. The wrapper returns -1 and stores a reason (here `EBADF`, "bad file descriptor") in the variable `errno`.

Key idea: A system call that fails is an ordinary return value, not a crash. The kernel checks every argument it receives, because it cannot trust anything that comes from user mode.

Watch out: Always check the return value. `write` can also return fewer bytes than requested (a short write), for example on a full pipe, so a robust program loops until everything is written.

cards.title: What is a **trap table**, and who sets it up?
cards.body:
A table that tells the CPU which kernel handler to run for each kind of trap, set up by the kernel at boot.

When a trap, interrupt or exception happens, the hardware looks up the handler's address in the table and jumps to it in kernel mode. A user program can only trigger a trap; it can never choose where the kernel code starts.

Why: Loading the trap table is a **privileged instruction**, one that works only in kernel mode. If a program could change the table, it could point a trap at its own code and run it in kernel mode. Trying a privileged instruction in user mode raises an exception, and the kernel stops the program.

Example: On RISC-V, a single register (`stvec` in S mode) holds the handler address and a cause register (`scause`) says why the trap happened. An Arm Cortex-M instead has a vector table in memory with one entry per exception number.
cards.searchQuery: trap table privileged instruction kernel boot handler

cards.title: What is a **context switch**?
cards.body:
Saving the registers of the running process or thread and loading those of another, so the CPU carries on with the other one.

The kernel stores the registers (including the program counter and stack pointer) in a record for the old process, loads the next process's registers and returns from the trap. To the next process it looks as if it had never stopped.

Why it matters: A context switch is pure overhead, since no program makes progress while it happens. Switching to another process also changes the address space, which can leave the caches and the TLB holding the old process's entries. That follow-on cost is often larger than the register copying itself.

Example: A timer interrupt arrives while process A runs. The handler saves A's registers, picks B, loads B's registers and returns, and B continues where it last stopped.
cards.searchQuery: context switch save restore registers process overhead

cards.title: How does a **timer interrupt** let the OS take the CPU back from a program that never makes a system call?
cards.body:
A hardware timer fires every few milliseconds, the trap table sends the CPU into a kernel handler, and the kernel may switch to another process (preemption).

An **interrupt** is a signal from hardware outside the running program that makes the CPU stop between two instructions and run a handler. The timer is set up by the kernel at boot, and the program cannot switch it off because that takes a privileged instruction.

This is **limited direct execution**: programs run straight on the CPU at full speed, and the kernel steps in only on traps. Taking the CPU away from a running process is called preemption.

Example: A user program stuck in `while (1) { }` does not freeze a desktop computer. The next timer interrupt brings the kernel in, and it runs other processes.

Watch out: A microcontroller running bare-metal firmware has no such protection, because nothing preempts the loop. A hung loop there stops everything unless a watchdog timer resets the chip.
cards.searchQuery: timer interrupt preemption limited direct execution OS regain CPU

cards.title: Why is it false that an **exception** always means the program has a bug?
cards.body:
An exception is just a trap caused by the instruction being run, and many are normal: system calls and page faults happen all the time in healthy programs.

An **exception** is synchronous: it comes from the instruction that is executing. An interrupt is asynchronous: it arrives from outside (a timer, a network card) at any time and has nothing to do with the current instruction.

A **fault** is an exception where the instruction could not complete, such as a page fault, or an integer divide by zero on x86. The handler may fix the cause and run the instruction again.

Example: When a program touches a page that is valid but not yet in RAM, the page-fault handler loads it and the instruction is retried; the program never notices. Only an access that can't be fixed, such as an invalid address, ends in a crash.

Key idea: Three ways into the kernel: an interrupt (asynchronous, from hardware), a fault (synchronous, the instruction couldn't finish) and a system call (synchronous and deliberate).
cards.searchQuery: interrupt versus exception fault system call synchronous asynchronous

cards.body:
139

The store to address 0 has no mapping in the page table, so the MMU raises a page fault. The kernel's fault handler finds that the address is not valid for this process and sends it the signal SIGSEGV (signal number 11). The default action for SIGSEGV is to terminate the process, and the shell reports a program killed by a signal as the exit code 128 plus the signal number: $128 + 11 = 139$.

Why it matters: This is a fault turned into a signal. The hardware detects the bad access, the kernel decides what it means, and the program only learns about it if it installs a signal handler.

Tip: `volatile` stops the compiler from deleting the store. Dereferencing a null pointer is undefined behavior, so an optimizing compiler may remove it or build something different.

cards.title: What is a **thread**, and how does it differ from a process?
cards.body:
A thread is one flow of execution inside a process: it has its own program counter, registers and stack, but shares the process's address space with its sibling threads.

A process with several threads is **multithreaded**. All its threads see the same code, global variables, heap and open files, but each thread has its own registers and its own stack.

Why it matters: Switching between threads of one process does not change the address space, so it is cheaper than switching between processes. Sharing data is also easy: threads just use the same variables.

Watch out: The sharing is also the danger. One thread's wild pointer can corrupt another thread's data, a crash in one thread ends the whole process, and unprotected updates to shared variables cause bugs (see the Race conditions unit).
cards.searchQuery: thread definition shared address space own stack registers versus process

cards.title: What is the difference between **concurrency** and **parallelism**?
cards.body:
Concurrency means several tasks are in progress during overlapping time periods, perhaps taking turns on one core; parallelism means several tasks actually run at the same instant on different cores.

Example: Two threads on a single-core microcontroller are concurrent: the scheduler switches between them, so both make progress, but never at the same instant. On a dual-core chip they can also be parallel.

Why it matters: Parallelism makes work finish sooner. Concurrency is about structure: handling several activities, such as a sensor, a display and a radio, in one program.

Watch out: Concurrency bugs do not need multiple cores. On one core the scheduler can still pause a thread between any two instructions and run another, so shared data can be corrupted even without parallelism.
cards.searchQuery: concurrency versus parallelism difference single core threads

cards.body:
`thread`, then `main`, in that order every time.

**POSIX threads** (**pthreads**) is the standard C interface for threads. `pthread_create(&t, NULL, work, arg)` starts a new thread that runs `work(arg)`; the thread's ID is stored in `t`. `pthread_join(t, NULL)` blocks the caller until that thread has finished.

Because `main` joins before its `printf`, the thread's line must come first.

Watch out: If `main` returned without joining, the whole process would end and could kill the thread before it printed anything. Every thread you create should be joined.

cards.body:
`42`

`x` is a local variable on `main`'s stack, but the new thread lives in the same address space, so the pointer `&x` is valid there and the thread writes straight into `x`.

This is the sharing that threads give you for free, and a separate process would not have. The `pthread_join` guarantees the write has happened before `main` reads `x`.

Watch out: A pointer to a local variable is only valid while that function's frame exists. Here `main` waits in `pthread_join`, so the frame stays alive. If `main` returned first, the thread would write into dead stack memory.

cards.title: Why does every **thread** need its own **stack**?
cards.body:
A stack holds a thread's call history (local variables, return addresses and saved registers), and two threads are at different points in different calls.

Example: Thread A is inside `f` called from `g`, while thread B is inside `h`. If they shared one stack, each call would push frames on top of the other's, and the first return would pop the wrong return address.

When a thread is created, the OS or library sets aside a block of memory in the process's address space for its stack. The size is fixed when the thread starts, unlike the main thread's stack, which the OS can grow up to a limit.

Watch out: Two threads running the same function do not share its local variables. Each has its own copy in its own frame, which is why locals are safe from other threads, while globals and heap objects are not.
cards.searchQuery: why each thread has its own stack call frames local variables

cards.title: A microcontroller with 64 KiB of RAM runs eight threads. Should you give every thread the same generous $8\,\mathrm{KiB}$ stack?
cards.body:
No: size each stack from its measured worst-case use plus a safety margin; eight 8 KiB stacks would use all 64 KiB.

The arithmetic is $8 \times 8\,\mathrm{KiB} = 64\,\mathrm{KiB}$, which leaves nothing for globals, the heap or the kernel. Too small a stack is just as bad: an overflow silently overwrites whatever lies next to it, unless a memory protection unit guards it.

Tip: Measure instead of guessing. Fill each stack with a known pattern, run the worst case and see how much was touched (many small kernels report this as the stack's high-water mark). Add a margin, and avoid recursion and big local arrays in threaded code.

Watch out: The other side holds on a desktop. A 64-bit Linux thread typically gets an 8 MiB stack by default (the `ulimit -s` limit), but with virtual memory only the pages actually touched use RAM, so generous stacks are cheap there.

refs: Linux man page pthread_create(3), section Notes

cards.body:
Either `A` then `B`, or `B` then `A`; which one you get can change from run to run.

Both threads are ready as soon as they are created, and the scheduler decides which runs first. That is **nondeterminism**: the same program with the same input can behave differently on different runs.

Creating `a` before `b` does not make `a` print first. Each line comes out whole, because `printf` locks the output stream while it runs, so the two lines never mix.

Watch out: A test that passes ten times proves little, since a rare interleaving may appear only on the eleventh run or on faster hardware. Concurrent code has to be correct for every possible interleaving.

cards.body:
All three threads receive a pointer to the same variable `i`, which the loop keeps changing, so the threads print unpredictable values, often `3 3 3`.

A new thread may not start running until after `main` has moved on. By then `i` has changed, and the thread reads its current value through the pointer. (Run on one Apple laptop, this printed mixes such as `2 3 3`, `1 3 3` and `3 3 3`.)

Fix: Give each thread its own storage, for example `int id[3];`, set `id[i] = i;` and pass `&id[i]`. Another way is to pass the number itself as the pointer value, with a cast.

Key idea: Pass a pointer to a value only if that value stays unchanged and alive for as long as the thread might read it.

cards.title: In CPU scheduling, what is a job's **turnaround time**? (The **scheduler** is the part of the kernel that picks what runs next.)
cards.body:
Turnaround time $=$ completion time $-$ arrival time: how long the job takes from the moment it arrives until it finishes.

Example: A job arrives at $t = 0$ ms, first gets the CPU at $t = 5$ ms and finishes at $t = 15$ ms. Its turnaround time is $15 - 0 = 15$ ms.

Why it matters: Turnaround time is the natural measure for batch work, such as a build or a data-processing job, where only the finishing time counts. The average over all jobs is the usual score for comparing schedulers.

Watch out: Turnaround time includes all the waiting, not only the time actually spent running. A job that needs 10 ms of CPU can have a turnaround time of 100 ms.
cards.searchQuery: turnaround time scheduling completion minus arrival

cards.title: In CPU scheduling, what is a job's **response time**?
cards.body:
Response time $=$ first-run time $-$ arrival time: how long the job waits from arriving until it first gets the CPU.

Example: A job arrives at $t = 0$ ms, first runs at $t = 5$ ms and finishes at $t = 15$ ms. Its response time is $5 - 0 = 5$ ms, while its turnaround time is 15 ms.

Why it matters: Response time is what an interactive user feels. A key press that waits 200 ms before anything reacts seems broken, even if the work itself is quick.

Key idea: A scheduler that is good at turnaround is often poor at response time, and the other way round. Scheduling is mostly about balancing the two.
cards.searchQuery: response time scheduling first run minus arrival interactive

cards.title: Jobs A, B and C all arrive at time $0$ and need $100$, $10$ and $10$ ms of CPU. **FIFO scheduling** runs each job to completion in arrival order (A, B, C). **Shortest job first** (SJF) runs the shortest waiting job to completion. What is the average turnaround time under each?
cards.body:
FIFO: $110$ ms. SJF: $50$ ms.

FIFO: A finishes at 100, B at 110, C at 120, so the average is $(100 + 110 + 120)/3 = 110$ ms.

SJF: the order is B, C, A. B finishes at 10, C at 20 and A at 120, so the average is $(10 + 20 + 120)/3 = 50$ ms.

Why: With FIFO, the two short jobs are stuck behind the long one, called the convoy effect. SJF runs short jobs first, which gives the lowest possible average turnaround when all jobs arrive together.

Watch out: SJF needs to know each job's length in advance, which a real OS usually does not. It can also starve a long job if short ones keep arriving.
cards.searchQuery: FIFO versus shortest job first average turnaround convoy effect

cards.title: Three jobs each need $5$ ms of CPU and all arrive at time $0$. **Round robin** runs each ready job for one **time slice** (also called a quantum), then moves to the next, in the order A, B, C, A, B, C, and so on. With a $1$ ms slice and no switching cost, what are the average response time and the average turnaround time? Compare with FIFO.
cards.body:
Round robin: average response $1$ ms, average turnaround $14$ ms. FIFO: $5$ ms and $10$ ms.

Round robin: A, B and C first run at 0, 1 and 2 ms, so the average response time is $1$ ms. The jobs finish at 13, 14 and 15 ms, so the average turnaround is $(13 + 14 + 15)/3 = 14$ ms.

FIFO: the jobs first run at 0, 5 and 10 ms (average $5$ ms) and finish at 5, 10 and 15 ms (average $10$ ms).

Key idea: Round robin trades turnaround for response time. When jobs are equally long, it stretches every job out, so the finishing times get worse, but nobody waits long for a first turn.
cards.searchQuery: round robin time slice average response turnaround compared FIFO

cards.title: A context switch costs $10\,\mu\mathrm{s}$. Roughly what share of CPU time is lost to switching with a $20\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ slice and with a $1\,\mathrm{ms}$ slice, and which suits an interactive system?
cards.body:
About $33\%$ is lost with $20\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ slices and about $1\%$ with $1\,\mathrm{ms}$ slices, so an interactive system should pick a slice of a few milliseconds.

The overhead share is switch cost divided by (slice + switch cost): $10/(20+10) \approx 33\%$ and $10/(1000+10) \approx 1\%$.

The other side: Longer slices waste less time but hurt response. With 10 ready jobs and $100\,\mathrm{ms}$ slices, a newly arrived job can wait about $10 \times 100\,\mathrm{ms} = 1\,\mathrm{s}$ before its first turn.

Tip: Choose the slice well above the switch cost, so the overhead is a percent or so, but short enough that the number of ready jobs times the slice is still a delay people cannot notice. The switch cost here is an assumed round number.
cards.searchQuery: time slice length trade-off context switch overhead response time

cards.title: What is **starvation** in scheduling, and how does **priority scheduling** cause it?
cards.body:
Starvation is a ready job that never gets the CPU; priority scheduling always runs the highest-priority ready job, so low-priority jobs starve while higher-priority work keeps arriving.

Example: A logging task with the lowest priority never runs on a device whose higher-priority tasks always have something to do.

Why it matters: Starvation is not a bug inside the starved job. It follows from how the scheduler chooses. The usual cure is **aging**: raise a job's priority the longer it waits, so that it eventually wins.

Tip: Real systems that must keep deadlines accept starvation of low-priority work on purpose and instead limit how much CPU time the high-priority work may use.
cards.searchQuery: starvation priority scheduling low priority never runs aging

cards.title: How does a **multi-level feedback queue** (MLFQ) scheduler treat new jobs, jobs that use up their time allotment, and long-waiting jobs?
cards.body:
New jobs start in the top queue; a job that uses up its allotment drops one queue; the scheduler runs the highest non-empty queue (round robin within it) and periodically moves every job back to the top.

An MLFQ keeps several queues of different priority. A job that gives up the CPU early, for example to wait for the keyboard, stays high, so interactive jobs get quick responses. A job that uses its whole allotment is treated as a CPU hog and sinks, and it still gets the CPU when nothing above it is ready.

Why it works: The scheduler does not need to know job lengths. It learns from behavior, and approximates shortest job first for short jobs while still running long ones.

Key idea: The periodic boost to the top queue solves two problems: it prevents starvation of low queues, and it lets a job that has become interactive be treated that way again.

Watch out: If a job's allotment resets whenever it yields, it can yield just before its slice ends and stay on top forever. Real designs count the total time used at each level.
cards.searchQuery: multi-level feedback queue rules priority boost allotment

cards.title: A desktop-style scheduler shares the CPU fairly among tasks, while a real-time scheduler always runs the highest-priority ready task. Which fits a motor-control task with a hard deadline of $1\,\mathrm{ms}$?
cards.body:
Fixed-priority preemptive scheduling, with the motor task at the highest priority, because its deadline must hold no matter what else is ready.

Under a fair scheduler the motor task is one of many that share the CPU, so a burst of other work can delay it past its deadline. With fixed priorities, whenever the motor task is ready it preempts everything else, so its delay is bounded.

The other side: Fair schedulers are good for general computing: they keep everything responsive and nothing starves. Fixed-priority scheduling can starve low-priority tasks, so the designer must make sure the high-priority tasks use only a small, known share of the CPU.

Example: Linux offers both: its normal policy shares time fairly, and its `SCHED_FIFO` and `SCHED_RR` policies are fixed-priority real-time classes. Small real-time kernels such as FreeRTOS use fixed priorities by default and round robin among tasks of equal priority.
cards.searchQuery: fixed priority real-time scheduling versus fair share desktop scheduler deadline

cards.title: What is a **race condition**?
cards.body:
A bug where the result depends on the timing of how threads interleave.

When threads touch the same data, the outcome can depend on which one gets there first, and that can change from run to run because scheduling is nondeterministic.

Example: Two threads each add 1 to a shared counter that holds 5. The correct result is 7, but a bad interleaving leaves 6, because one update overwrote the other (a lost update).

Watch out: Race conditions are hard to find because the program usually works. The bad interleaving may need a rare timing, so tests pass and the bug shows up later in the field.
cards.searchQuery: race condition definition timing threads lost update
refs: CS:APP 3e, §12.4 Shared Variables in Threaded Programs

cards.title: What is a **critical section**, and which variables in it are **shared variables**?
cards.body:
A critical section is a stretch of code that touches shared state and must not be run by more than one thread at a time; the shared variables are those that more than one thread can access.

Example: In `balance = balance + amount;` the statement is the critical section, and the global `balance` is the shared variable. The local variable `amount` lives on the calling thread's own stack, so no other thread can see it.

Why it matters: Finding the critical sections is the first step in making threaded code safe. Once found, you make sure only one thread is inside at a time (mutual exclusion), using the tools of the next unit.

Tip: Look for globals, heap objects and anything reached through a pointer that was passed to several threads. Local variables are private unless their address was handed to another thread.
cards.searchQuery: critical section shared variable mutual exclusion definition
refs: CS:APP 3e, §12.4 Shared Variables in Threaded Programs

cards.title: Why is it false that `counter++` is safe between threads because it is a single line of C?
cards.body:
One line of C can compile to several instructions (load, add, store), and another thread can run between them, so an update can be lost.

On RISC-V, `counter++` on a shared 32-bit `int` becomes roughly: `lw t0, 0(a0)`, then `addi t0, t0, 1`, then `sw t0, 0(a0)`.

Example: Let `counter` be 5. Thread 1 loads 5. Thread 2 then loads 5 as well. Thread 1 stores 6, and thread 2 stores 6. Two increments ran, but the counter went up by one.

Watch out: Even on a chip with a single "add to memory" instruction, the instruction is a read followed by a write inside the hardware. Unless it is explicitly atomic, another core can slip in between, so the line is still not safe.
cards.searchQuery: counter++ not atomic load add store lost update threads

cards.body:
Usually a number well below $2{,}000{,}000$, and a different one on each run. It is not reliably $2{,}000{,}000$.

Each `counter++` is a load, an add and a store, and the two threads overwrite each other's results. One run on an Apple laptop printed values just above $1{,}000{,}000$.

The program has a **data race**: two threads access the same memory location with plain (non-atomic) accesses, at least one access is a write, and nothing orders them. In C11 a data race is undefined behavior, so the compiler is allowed to assume it never happens.

Watch out: With `-O2` the compiler may keep `counter` in a register for the whole loop and add once, so some builds print exactly $2{,}000{,}000$ by luck. The race is still there. Also, a race condition need not be a data race, but every data race is a bug.

cards.title: What does an **atomic instruction** guarantee, and how do **test-and-set**, **compare-and-swap** and RISC-V **LR/SC** work?
cards.body:
It performs a read-modify-write as one indivisible step, so no other thread or core ever sees or interleaves with half of it.

- **Test-and-set** writes 1 to a location and returns the old value. Only the first caller gets 0 back.
- **Compare-and-swap** (CAS) takes an address, an expected value and a new value: it writes the new value only if the location still holds the expected one, and tells you whether it did.
- **LR/SC** is RISC-V's pair: `lr.w` loads a word and marks it as reserved; `sc.w` stores only if no one has written that address since, and puts 0 in its result register on success, non-zero on failure. You retry in a loop.

Key idea: **Atomicity** means all-or-nothing as seen by other threads. These instructions are the hardware that mutexes and atomic counters are built from.

Watch out: One atomic instruction protects one memory word. A critical section of several steps, or one that updates two variables together, still needs a lock.
cards.searchQuery: atomic instruction test-and-set compare-and-swap RISC-V LR SC
refs: RISC-V Unprivileged ISA manual, ch. 'A' extension

cards.body:
`2000000`, on every run.

`atomic_fetch_add(&counter, 1)` is one atomic read-modify-write, so the two threads can never overwrite each other's update, and all $2 \times 1{,}000{,}000$ increments are counted. It compiles to a single atomic instruction, such as `lock xadd` on x86 or `amoadd` on RISC-V, or to a load-reserved/store-conditional retry loop.

Why it matters: This is the cheap fix for a shared counter. It is also the building block for flags, statistics and sequence numbers.

Watch out: Atomic operations are slower than plain ones when several cores fight over the same variable. And the atomicity covers only that one variable: two separate atomic updates together are not a critical section.

cards.body:
The compare-and-swap fails: it leaves `x` alone, returns false and copies the current value of `x` into `old`; the loop then tries again with `old + 1` computed from that new value.

On success (`x` still equals `old`), `x` becomes `old + 1` and the loop ends. So `x` only changes when nobody interfered between reading it and updating it.

Why it works: Failure means someone else got in first, and nothing was lost, because we had not written anything yet. The retry sees the newer value and builds on it. This pattern, read, compute, then CAS and retry on failure, can update a value without ever holding a lock.

Tip: The same idea is what a RISC-V LR/SC loop does: `lr.w`, compute, `sc.w`, and branch back if `sc.w` reports failure.

cards.title: What is a **mutex** (a **lock**), and what do `pthread_mutex_lock` and `pthread_mutex_unlock` do?
cards.body:
A mutual-exclusion lock that only one thread can hold at a time: `pthread_mutex_lock` takes it, blocking until it is free, and `pthread_mutex_unlock` releases it.

You wrap each critical section in a lock and an unlock of the same mutex, so only one thread at a time runs the code in between. A thread that finds the mutex held is **blocked**: the kernel parks it in the blocked state and it uses no CPU until the holder unlocks.

A mutex declared with `PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER` is ready to use.

Watch out: A mutex protects data only by agreement. Every access to the shared variable, in every thread, must take the same mutex. One unprotected access, or two different mutexes guarding the same data, brings the race back.

cards.body:
`2000000`, on every run.

Each increment sits between `pthread_mutex_lock` and `pthread_mutex_unlock`, so the load, add and store of one thread can never overlap with another's. Nothing is lost.

Why it works: Unlocking also makes the thread's write visible to the next thread that locks, so the second thread always starts from the newest value.

Tip: Locking a million times is far slower than the increments themselves. If a thread can finish a whole batch of work under one lock acquisition, that is faster, as long as the other threads can wait that long. This choice is the lock granularity (see the card on it).

cards.body:
When the buffer is full, `push` returns without unlocking, so the mutex stays locked forever and every later call blocks in `pthread_mutex_lock`.

Fix: Release the lock on every path out of the function, for example `pthread_mutex_unlock(&m); return -1;` in the full case, or use a single exit point at the bottom.

Why it matters: Early `return`, `break` and `goto` statements, and error handling, are the usual way a lock gets forgotten. The program then hangs far from the bug, and only after the buffer has filled up.

Tip: C++ has a neat answer: a scope guard such as `std::lock_guard` (RAII) unlocks in its destructor, so every way out of the scope releases the mutex.

cards.title: When should you use a **spinlock** instead of a **blocking** lock such as a mutex?
cards.body:
Use a spinlock when the critical section is very short, the holder is running on another core, and the code cannot sleep; use a blocking lock otherwise.

A spinlock waits by looping on an atomic instruction such as test-and-set until the lock is free. A blocking lock puts the waiting thread to sleep and wakes it later.

Why spinning wins sometimes: Sleeping and waking cost a trip through the kernel and two context switches, which is far more than a critical section of a few instructions. An interrupt handler also has no process to put to sleep, so it can only spin.

The other side: Spinning burns CPU. On a single core it is worse than useless: the holder cannot run while the waiter spins, so the waiter wastes its whole time slice. With a long critical section, or a holder that may itself be preempted, block instead.

Example: On a single-core Cortex-M, the usual lock for data shared with an interrupt handler is to switch interrupts off briefly. That is a spin-free, very short critical section.
cards.searchQuery: spinlock versus mutex blocking lock when to use short critical section

cards.title: What is **lock granularity**, and what is the trade-off between one coarse lock and many fine-grained locks?
cards.body:
Granularity is how much data one lock protects: a coarse lock protects a lot and is simple but serializes work; fine-grained locks each protect a little, so more work runs in parallel but the code is harder to get right.

Example: A hash table with 64 buckets. One lock for the whole table is easy and safe, but every operation waits for every other one. One lock per bucket lets threads that touch different buckets run at the same time.

The costs of fine-grained locking: more locks to store, more lock operations, and operations that need several buckets at once (such as resizing the table) must take many locks, in a careful order, or they can hang (see the Deadlock unit).

Tip: Start coarse, measure, and refine only where the lock is a real bottleneck. A simple, correct program is easier to speed up than a fast, subtly wrong one.
cards.searchQuery: lock granularity coarse fine-grained locking hash table trade-off

cards.title: What is a **condition variable**, and what do `pthread_cond_wait` and `pthread_cond_signal` do?
cards.body:
A queue where threads sleep until some condition becomes true: `pthread_cond_wait` releases the mutex and sleeps in one atomic step, `pthread_cond_signal` wakes one waiter, and the waiter holds the mutex again when `wait` returns.

A condition variable is always used with a mutex and with real data that describes the condition, such as `count > 0`. The condition variable itself stores no state.

Why releasing and sleeping must be one step: If a thread released the mutex first and then went to sleep, another thread could signal in between, and the wake-up would be lost.

Watch out: A signal sent when no thread is waiting is simply lost. That is why threads test the condition in the data first and wait only if it is false. Never rely on the signal alone.
cards.searchQuery: condition variable pthread_cond_wait signal definition mutex

cards.body:
The `if` must be a `while`: after waking, the condition may be false again, so the thread has to check it again before it uses the buffer.

Example: Consumer C1 is waiting. A producer adds one item and signals. C1 wakes up but has to reacquire the mutex first. Before it does, another consumer C2 arrives, locks the mutex, sees `count == 1` and takes the item. C1 then gets the mutex, skips the check and runs `count--`, leaving $-1$.

Fix: `while (count == 0) pthread_cond_wait(&filled, &m);` The thread goes back to sleep if someone else got the item first.

Why it matters: POSIX also allows spurious wake-ups, where `wait` returns although nobody signalled. A `while` loop makes the code correct in both cases.

cards.title: What is a counting **semaphore**, and what do `sem_wait` and `sem_post` do?
cards.searchQuery: counting semaphore sem_wait sem_post definition initial value

cards.body:
`empty` counts free slots, so it must start at `N` (4), not 0: with 0, the producer's first `sem_wait(&empty)` blocks at once, and the consumer waits for `full`, so nothing ever happens.

Fix: `sem_init(&empty, 0, N);` and keep `full` at 0. Then `empty + full = N` always holds: `put` waits for a free slot and announces a filled one, and `get` does the reverse.

Why it works: The semaphores make a full buffer block the producer and an empty buffer block the consumer, with no busy-waiting.

Watch out: With one producer and one consumer, `in` and `out` are each touched by one thread, so this is safe. With several producers or several consumers, the index updates need a mutex too, taken after the `sem_wait`, not before it: the other order can hang.

cards.body:
The semaphore starts at 1, so the parent's `sem_wait` succeeds immediately without waiting for the child; it should start at 0.

Fix: `sem_init(&done, 0, 0);` With 0, `sem_wait` blocks until the child's `sem_post` raises the count to 1, so `child` is always printed first.

Why it works: A semaphore with initial value 0 is a signal that something has happened. Its value counts events that have occurred but not yet been consumed, so it works even if the child posts before the parent waits.

Tip: Pick the initial value by asking how many units are available right now: a lock has 1, a signal has 0, and a pool of $N$ slots has $N$.

cards.title: What is a **deadlock**, and what four conditions must all hold for one to occur?
cards.body:
A deadlock is a state in which threads each hold something and wait for something another holds, so none can ever continue; it needs mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and a circular wait.

- Mutual exclusion: a resource (such as a mutex) is held by one thread at a time.
- Hold-and-wait: a thread keeps what it holds while it waits for more.
- No preemption: a held resource cannot be taken away; its holder must release it.
- **Circular wait**: there is a cycle of threads, each waiting for a resource held by the next.

Example: Thread 1 holds lock A and waits for lock B, while thread 2 holds B and waits for A. Neither can proceed, and the program hangs without crashing.

Key idea: Break any one of the four conditions and deadlock becomes impossible. In practice the easiest one to break is the circular wait.
cards.searchQuery: deadlock four conditions mutual exclusion hold and wait circular wait

cards.body:
Yes: thread 0 locks `m[0]` then `m[1]`, while thread 1 locks `m[1]` then `m[0]`. If each gets its first lock before the other gets its second, both wait forever. The fix is **lock ordering**: every thread takes the locks in the same global order, for example `m[0]` before `m[1]`.

The hang is not certain. Run it a few times and it usually finishes, because one thread often gets both locks before the other starts. That is why such bugs survive testing and appear later, under load.

Why it works: With a fixed order, a cycle of waiting threads cannot form, since a thread holding `m[1]` never waits for `m[0]`. This removes the circular-wait condition.

Tip: When the locks are different objects, order them by something stable, such as their address or an id number. Document the order next to the locks.

cards.title: To avoid deadlock in code that needs several locks at once, should you use a fixed lock order or replace them all with one big lock?
cards.body:
Use a fixed lock order when you need the parallelism of separate locks; use one big lock when the code is small and the contention is low.

One big lock cannot deadlock with itself, and it is simple to reason about. But every thread waits for every other one, which wastes the extra cores.

With a fixed order, the threads that touch different data can run at the same time. The price is discipline: every code path, including future ones, must follow the order, and a single violation brings the hang back. The order is also hard to keep when the next lock to take depends on the data.

Tip: Start with the one big lock. Move to several locks with a documented order only after measurement shows the single lock to be a bottleneck.
cards.searchQuery: lock ordering versus single global lock deadlock avoidance trade-off

cards.title: What are an **atomicity violation** and an **order violation** in threaded code?
cards.body:
An atomicity violation is a group of accesses that was meant to run as one unit but isn't protected, so another thread slips in; an order violation is two accesses meant to happen in a certain order, with nothing enforcing it.

Example (atomicity): A thread checks `if (p->name != NULL)` and then uses `p->name`. Another thread sets it to `NULL` in between. Fix: hold one lock across the check and the use, and take the same lock where the other thread sets it to `NULL`.

Example (order): A worker thread reads a variable that `main` has not yet initialized, because `main` creates the thread first and assigns the variable after. Fix: initialize before creating the thread, or make the worker wait on a condition variable or semaphore until the data is ready.

Why it matters: Studies of real concurrency bugs in large programs found that most non-deadlock bugs were of these two kinds, and a lock alone cures only the first.

cards.body:
A line starting `WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race`, with a stack trace for each of the two conflicting writes to `n` (the one in `f` and the one in `main`).

**ThreadSanitizer** (TSan) is a compiler tool, like AddressSanitizer: the compiler adds checks to each memory access, and at run time they notice two threads accessing the same location with no ordering between them. The report points at the exact source lines, which is why `-g` helps.

Both `n++` statements are unprotected writes to a shared variable. Protect them with a mutex, or make `n` atomic, and the warning goes away.

Watch out: TSan only sees races that actually happen in the run you make, so exercise the code with realistic inputs. It slows the program down several times and cannot be combined with AddressSanitizer in one build.

cards.title: What is **priority inversion**? Describe it with a high-, a medium- and a low-priority thread.
cards.body:
A high-priority thread is stuck waiting for a lock held by a low-priority thread, and a medium-priority thread keeps the low one from running, so the high-priority thread effectively waits for the medium one.

1. The low-priority thread L takes a mutex.
2. The high-priority thread H becomes ready, needs that mutex and blocks.
3. The medium-priority thread M, which doesn't use the mutex, becomes ready and, having higher priority than L, preempts it.
4. L can't run to release the mutex, so H waits as long as M runs.

Fix: **Priority inheritance**: while L holds the lock that H wants, L temporarily runs at H's priority, so M can no longer preempt it. POSIX offers this for mutexes through `PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT`.

Example: This problem made the 1997 Mars Pathfinder lander reset itself repeatedly until priority inheritance was switched on for the mutex involved.

cards.title: What three **device registers** make up the canonical interface between the CPU and an I/O device?
cards.body:
A status register (what the device is doing, and whether it is ready), a command register (what to do next) and a data register (the bytes going in or out).

A **device register** is a storage location inside the device that software reads and writes. On most microcontrollers the registers are memory-mapped, so a normal load or store reaches them.

Example: To send a byte, the driver reads the status register until the device is not busy, writes the byte to the data register, then writes the command register to start the transfer.

Watch out: Reading or writing a device register often has side effects that memory doesn't have. Reading the data register may remove the byte from the device's receive queue, so one read in the code must remain exactly one read in the machine code. That is why these registers are accessed through `volatile`.
cards.searchQuery: device registers status command data canonical device interface

cards.body:
The compiler may read `UART_STATUS` once, keep the value in a register, and reuse it every time round the loop, so the loop never sees the device change and spins forever.

This loop is **polling**: the CPU repeatedly reads the status register until the device is ready. Nothing in the program writes to that address, so without `volatile` an optimizing compiler is allowed to assume the value cannot change.

With `volatile`, each loop iteration performs a real load from the register. After the loop, reading `UART_DATA` also counts: on many devices that read takes the byte out of the receiver and clears the ready bit.

Watch out: A polling loop with no timeout hangs the firmware if the device never answers, for example when a cable is unplugged. Real drivers count iterations or check a timer.
cards.searchQuery: polling loop status register volatile compiler hoists read UART

cards.title: A UART at 115,200 baud (10 bits per byte) delivers a byte about every $87\,\mu\mathrm{s}$. For firmware that also does other work, should it read the UART by **polling** or by **interrupt-driven I/O**?
cards.body:
Interrupt-driven I/O: the device raises an interrupt when a byte arrives, and the CPU does other work until then.

The rate is $115200 / 10 = 11{,}520$ bytes per second, one byte every $1/11520\,\mathrm{s} \approx 87\,\mu\mathrm{s}$. To poll without losing bytes, the main loop would have to come back to the UART faster than that, whatever else it is doing. With interrupts, if entering and leaving the handler costs an assumed $2\,\mu\mathrm{s}$, only about $2/87 \approx 2\%$ of the time goes on the UART.

The other side: Polling wins when the device is almost always ready, because each interrupt then costs more than a quick status check, or when the CPU has nothing else to do and wants the lowest latency. High-speed network drivers often switch from interrupts to polling under heavy traffic for this reason.

Key idea: Interrupts pay a fixed cost per event, and polling pays a cost per check. Choose by how often the events come compared with the other work.
cards.searchQuery: polling versus interrupt driven I/O trade-off UART when to use

cards.title: What is **direct memory access** (DMA), and why does it speed up bulk transfers?
cards.body:
DMA is a hardware engine that copies data between a device and memory by itself; the CPU only sets up the transfer and gets an interrupt when it is done.

The driver tells the DMA controller the source, the destination and the length, then starts it. The CPU is free to run other code during the copy.

Example: Reading a 4 KiB block from a device word by word takes $4096 / 4 = 1024$ loads and stores by the CPU. With DMA the CPU does a few register writes and one interrupt.

Watch out: DMA writes memory behind the CPU's back, so the CPU's cache may still hold old data for the buffer. Drivers must invalidate or flush the cache for that range, or put the buffer in uncached memory. Devices also use physical addresses, not the process's virtual ones.

cards.title: What is a **device driver**?
cards.body:
The OS code that knows one kind of device's registers and quirks and presents it to the rest of the system through a standard interface.

The rest of the OS, and the programs above it, just ask to read or write; the driver turns that into register accesses, interrupts and DMA setup for the actual hardware. On Unix-like systems many devices appear as files, so a program uses the same `read` and `write` calls for a disk, a serial port or a sensor.

Why it matters: Without drivers, every program would have to contain code for every device. With them, a new device needs only a new driver.

Watch out: Drivers usually run in kernel mode, so a bug in a driver can crash the entire system, and driver bugs are a leading cause of OS failures. Firmware on microcontrollers has the same layering in its hardware abstraction layer.
cards.searchQuery: device driver definition OS abstraction hides device details

cards.body:
`key 5`, `timer 10`, `key 20`, `key 1`, then `total 36` (each on its own line). No lock is needed because only one thread exists and each handler runs to completion before the next event is taken.

An event loop waits for the next event (a key press, a timer tick, data on a socket) and calls the matching handler through a table of function pointers. Real loops block in a call such as `poll` or `select` until something is ready. This style is called event-based concurrency, and it is an alternative to threads.

Why it matters: Handlers never run at the same time, so shared data has no races. Many embedded programs are built this way (event-driven firmware).

Watch out: A handler that blocks, for example on a slow read, or computes for a long time, stalls every other event. The loop also uses only one core.
